title: Thou hast searched me (Psalm 138 [139])
hookLine: you knit me in my mother's womb, and there's nowhere God is not
tomorrow: let every spirit praise the Lord

cards: Some rooms in a life stay locked. A thing done at nineteen. A thought never said out loud.
The self that shows up at two in the morning. People let each other into the front hallway and keep the rest shut. Being fully known can be frightening.
Never being known at all can be lonely. Today's psalm stands right between the two. It says: you have been seen in every room, and you have not been walked out on.

teach.b: The title is the older English wording: thou hast searched me. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, says: "Lord, thou hast proved me, and known me." Proved, as in tested.
Under both is the Hebrew chaqar, to search out, to examine through and through. First, known.
The psalmist says God knows his sitting down and his rising up, understands his thoughts from far off, knows his ways before he takes them. That could sound like surveillance. It reads like wonder.

Second, nowhere God is not. In the Douay-Rheims: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend into heaven, thou art there: if I descend into hell, thou art present."
Up, down, the far end of the sea, the dark itself: the psalmist tries every exit and finds God already there, not to trap him but to hold him. Even darkness, he says, is not dark to you. Third, made.
"Thou hast protected me from my mother's womb," the Douay says, and the psalmist marvels at how he was formed before anyone saw him.
Before anyone else knew he existed, he was known. Catholics hear this psalm at Easter: the old entrance chant of Easter Sunday, Resurrexi, draws on a verse of it, I arose, and am still with thee.
And the psalm ends where it started, but now as a request: prove me, O God, and know my heart.

teach.h: IF I ASCEND INTO HEAVEN, THOU ART THERE.
teach.b: The knowing that could have been frightening becomes something he asks for.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 138 [139] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and a verse of it shapes the traditional entrance chant of Easter Sunday; some pray its closing lines before an examination of conscience.

o: to search out, to examine through and through
to hide away, to keep a thing secret
to judge and condemn after a trial

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: the psalm reads like God spying on the psalmist
it reads like wonder: known everywhere, and held, not trapped.
the psalmist tries every exit and finds God already there
heaven, hell, the far sea, the dark itself: "thou art there."
the psalm ends by asking to be searched
prove me, O God, and know my heart: what was frightening becomes a request.

games.q: you're the psalmist, and you realize there's nowhere you can go that God hasn't already seen. what do you do?
o: praise God for making you, and ask to be searched.
stop praying, since God already knows.
games.why: he marvels at being known from his mother's womb, and ends asking: prove me, O God, and know my heart.

practice: If there's a locked room in your own life, let yourself remember it's there; you don't have to open it or name it out loud.
If you pray, rest in the psalm's claim that God has already seen that room and hasn't left, and say its closing words: prove me, O God, and know my heart.
If you don't, simply breathe, and let yourself be all of who you are for two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Chaqar. Hebrew to search out, examine through, the root behind thou hast searched me, the psalm about being known completely, everywhere, and still held. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: you have searched me, from chaqar, to search out, examine through.

carryVoice: Your line: known, and not left. Every room seen, and nobody walked out. That's day one hundred ninety.
